As pointed out by the practitioners, there are significant positive impacts of adaptive lighting in terms of reduction in the negative impacts of lighting such as sky glow and in particular energy consumption. The crash and crime statics also showed that there was not a negative impact on crashes and crime, with the exception of the C1 class of roadways after midnight. Further investigation of the C1 roadways showed that this effect was not practically significant, as there were very few crashes to consider. The final consideration of the application of adaptive lighting was that of the public surveys. Generally, there was a lack of understanding about the impact of the adaptive lighting in cities with adaptive lighting. In Cambridge, the survey indicated that there was no significant impact on individual behaviors as a result of the adaptive system being used. These outcomes are similar to others found in similar investigations. These minimal negative impact results are significant in comparison to the energy consumption calculation that indicates that the energy savings can be as high as 55%. The final consideration is the recommendation for more public outreach, more buy-in from agency leadership, and more promotion of the adaptive lighting technology in the industry. 84 4.4.1 Recommendations for Phase 2 One consideration in the investigation was the understanding of how much the lighting should be varied. The 50% reduction from full output in the evening through the night was relatively unresearched and was based on the reduction in the pedestrian street usage in the IES documents. A human factors investigation should be undertaken to determine how low the lighting can be dimmed before impacting road user comfort and feelings of safety. 85 5 On-road Investigation of Lighting Metrics The primary goal of this task was to determine the light levels to which roadway lighting can be dimmed without compromising the perception of visibility, safety, and comfort of predominately pedestrian road users in residential areas. The secondary goal was to determine if there was any difference in the different commercially available light types (or CCTs) across these light levels. The third and final goal was to understand the pedestrians’ preferences and discomfort glare perceptions towards these light types and light levels.
